strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring degrees of human contribution in assisted writing. It explicitly focuses on informational contribution and acknowledges limitations concerning creative effort and legal authorship. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-m77ewjhu/call-8c9eb08dfe8c47ee9242e7b9b0b887bb/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The experiments cover four domains with 2,000 source items each, repeated generations, multiple generation and scoring models, and 2,500 WildChat examples. Consistent ordering from polishing to generation with brief prompts provides evidence that the score captures useful ordinal differences.
The core metric is simple and computable from token probabilities. Model identifiers, data sources, computational details, and a public code link provide a useful starting point for reproduction.
weaknesses: The interpretation as a percentage of human-contributed information exceeds what the derivation establishes. Definition 1 normalizes a pointwise likelihood gain, which becomes negative whenever p(y|x) < p(y); negative scores also appear in Figure 7. Consequently, the nonnegative shared-information interpretation illustrated in Figure 1 is not generally justified. Neither the derivation nor the ordinal experiments establish that numerical scores represent calibrated attribution percentages.

The output-only extension has a substantive gap between its definition and solution. Equations (7)–(9) derive a lower bound under a chosen plausibility threshold, but Equation (10) substitutes this bound for the minimum without establishing tightness or evaluating estimation error. Writing H = I(y)/N reveals that the estimator is simply 1 + log(tau)/H, a monotonic transformation of unconditional perplexity for fixed tau. Its interpretation as information necessarily supplied by humans therefore requires substantially stronger justification. Threshold selection and sensitivity are also insufficiently established.

The reported 97.4% human agreement concerns 1,000 pairs selected specifically because the proposed metric separates them by more than 0.1. This supports agreement on that filtered subset, but cannot establish performance on unselected comparisons or the ambiguous cases motivating the paper. An evaluation sampled independently of the metric, including comparisons within generation categories, is needed.

The empirical validation primarily demonstrates expected ordering among categories that also differ substantially in prompt length and textual overlap. No comparisons against input/output length ratios, lexical or semantic overlap, or unconditional perplexity are reported. Matched controls are needed to establish what the proposed measure contributes beyond these simpler proxies. WildChat category differences likewise provide plausibility evidence rather than independent attribution labels.
The robustness experiments test only two fixed prompt additions. They support narrow conclusions about those perturbations, while leaving resistance to score-directed manipulation unestablished.

Reproducibility cannot be fully assessed from the supplied material: exact prompts, sampling details, and annotation instructions are deferred to supplementary information that is absent from the provided PDF. Annotator counts and agreement are also not reported there. Despite the promising ordinal results, the interpretation, estimator, and validation gaps prevent a positive Findings recommendation. Correcting the claims and supplying stronger independent evaluation would justify reconsideration in the next cycle.
